title: Brazil pop fan groups rally for Lula in election runoff against Flávio Bolsonaro
content: Brazil’s famously outspoken fandoms have near-unanimously rallied behind the leftwing presidential candidate. On the streets of São Paulo, they explain their mission Earlier this month, Brazil’s president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva led a rally in São Paulo, as he aims to be re-elected to a fourth presidential term, and faces serious opposition from right-winger Flávio Bolsonaro. Taking the mic before a crowd on Avenida Paulista that organisers put at more than a million, the former union leader began: “I’m not sure whether to open this speech with ‘comrades’ or ‘fandoms from all over Brazil’.” The rally was organised by Lula’s Workers’ party (PT) and a string of other leftwing groups – but the spark came from pop music fandoms. More than 600 Brazilian fanbase groups for Billie Eilish, Lady Gaga, Katseye, Demi Lovato, Harry Styles, Katy Perry, Selena Gomez, as well as Brazilian stars such as Anitta, Marina Sena and Ludmilla among others, all came together to back Lula, waging an intense online campaign as soon as Lula’s rival, son of imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro, came out on top in the first round on 4 October. Neither candidate earned more than 50% of the vote, so a runoff is now scheduled for 25 October to decide between the two.
summary: More than 600 Brazilian fanbase groups for international and local pop stars have united to support leftwing candidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. This organized support emerged after Flávio Bolsonaro led the first round of voting, triggering a runoff scheduled for October 25.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Lawrence Wright's book 'Redemption' examines Texas death row women and nuns
content: The Pulitzer prize-winning writer’s new book looks at the women on death row in Texas and the nuns who have been trying to help them It is “stunning”, the Pulitzer-winning reporter Lawrence Wright said, that Redemption, his new book about women on death row in Texas and the nuns who minister to them, turns out to be published at a time of intense focus on capital punishment. Two cases dominate headlines: the Trump administration’s abandoned plan to livestream the firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009, and Tennessee’s failure to kill the convicted murderer Christa Pike by lethal injection. Away from the headlines, in Texas and elsewhere, executions continue.
summary: Lawrence Wright's new book 'Redemption' focuses on women on death row in Texas and the nuns who minister to them. The book was published amid heightened attention to capital punishment, including the Trump administration's plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan and Tennessee's failure to execute Christa Pike.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Tom Cruise film Digger is a commercial flop but praised as a climate change epic
content:
Alejandro González Iñárritu’s new film, Digger, starring Tom Cruise, has been described as a bombastic and misanthropic epic that is both a commercial flop and a critically savaged work. Despite its poor reception, the movie is characterized as a near-perfect climate change film for the current era. The narrative follows Digger Rockwell, a Texas oilman portrayed as a blunt caricature who remains indifferent to the environmental destruction caused by his drilling activities.

The protagonist’s actions trigger a disastrous splitting of the Arctic ice sheet, releasing a massive iceberg five times the size of Washington DC. This ice formation barrels toward Europe, threatening to cause a devastating tsunami. The film uses this catastrophic scenario to highlight the consequences of industrial negligence in the face of climate change.
summary: The new Alejandro González Iñárritu film Digger is described as a commercially unsuccessful but near-perfect climate change movie. The plot follows Tom Cruise's character, an oilman whose drilling triggers a massive iceberg threatening Europe.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Christina Applegate Reveals Misdiagnosis of Multiple Sclerosis on Podcast
content: The Married … with Children actor says the news is ‘unnerving’ and ‘really confusing’ Sign up for the Breaking News US newsletter email After becoming a prominent advocate for multiple sclerosis awareness and chronicling her struggles in an emotional memoir published in March, the Emmy-winning actor Christina Applegate has revealed she does not have the debilitating autoimmune disease after all. Applegate, 54, made the stunning announcement in an episode of her podcast MeSsy, recorded with fellow actor Jamie-Lynn Sigler, posted to YouTube on Tuesday.
summary: Actor Christina Applegate announced on her podcast that she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis. She described the news as unnerving and confusing after previously advocating for the disease in a memoir.

title: Jon Stewart on JD Vance’s rhetoric on immigrants: ‘cornerstone and intentional strategy’
content: Late-night hosts mocked JD Vance’s apology for “imperfect” rhetoric condemning immigrants and riots in France. The hosts also ridiculed the extremely brief tenure of White House press secretary Katie Zacharia.

title: Angel Reese's 30-point double-double helps Dream even WNBA finals
content:
Angel Reese recorded a 30-point, 16-rebound double-double to lead the Atlanta Dream to a 79-65 victory over the Golden State Valkyries, leveling the WNBA finals series at 1-1. The Dream emerged from the second half of the previous game’s defeat, with Reese raising her game in front of the Valkyries’ home crowd.

During the matchup, Reese explicitly communicated to her teammates, “I need the ball! I need the ball!” The Atlanta star’s performance was pivotal in securing the win, which evened the series after the Valkyries were outplayed in the latter portion of the contest.
summary: Angel Reese scored 30 points and grabbed 16 rebounds to lead the Atlanta Dream to a 79-65 victory over the Golden State Valkyries. The win levels the WNBA finals series at 1-1 after Atlanta outplayed the Valkyries in the second half.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Rays beat Guardians 7-3 to reach first World Series against Brewers
content:
The Tampa Bay Rays have secured a spot in the World Series, where they will face the Milwaukee Brewers in a matchup between two franchises seeking their first-ever championship. The Rays clinched their berth by defeating the Cleveland Guardians 7-3 in Game 6 of the American League Championship Series on Monday night, marking their third appearance in the World Series during the franchise’s 29 seasons.

Freddy Peralta anchored the pitching staff with 5.1 gritty innings, while Junior Caminero and Yandy Díaz each contributed two-run home runs to power the offense. The victory allowed the Rays to advance despite the Guardians’ efforts, setting the stage for a historic showdown against Milwaukee, which is also pursuing its initial World Series title.

The game was played in front of a sellout crowd of 40,230 fans at Tropicana Field. Supporters waved yellow-and-blue rally towels, rang cowbells, and chanted “Let’s go Rays!” throughout the evening. The stadium recently underwent significant renovations to repair extensive damage caused by Hurricane Milton, which had shredded the roof two years prior.
summary: The Tampa Bay Rays defeated the Cleveland Guardians 7-3 in Game 6 of the American League Championship Series to advance to the World Series. They will face the Milwaukee Brewers, as both teams are seeking to win their first-ever World Series championship.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Brazilian women’s football final sees São Paulo win as players warn against far‑right
content:
Female footballers, including goalkeepers Carlinha and Tayla Carolina, have voiced opposition to the far-right, expressing fears that a victory could negatively impact women’s football and broader society. The political tension surfaced during the Brazilian Women’s Championship final at Estádio do Morumbi, the day before the first round of elections. In that match, São Paulo drew 1-1 with Corinthians to claim the Brasileirão Women’s title with a 3-2 aggregate score.

Following the high-profile final, which attracted a record television audience of 23 million, goalkeeper Carlinha used a post-match interview to address her fans. She explicitly called for “Never again Bolsonaro in power,” linking the political outcome to the future of the sport and social conditions in Brazil.
summary: Brazilian women’s football final sees São Paulo win as players warn against far‑right.

title: Kulusevski returns for Tottenham as Davies goal lifts Spurs to 16th
content:
Dejan Kulusevski returned to the Tottenham Hotspur squad after a 526-day absence, making his first appearance for the club since 11 May 2025. During his match against Coventry, Kulusevski was part of a side that secured a narrow victory, aided by a late deflected goal from Ben Davies. This result moved Tottenham up to 16th place in the league standings.

The article notes that significant changes have occurred during Kulusevski’s time away, yet certain aspects remain consistent. When Kulusevski last played for Spurs, the team was in 17th position, a ranking they also finished with in both the 2024-25 season and the 2025-26 season. The piece highlights this continuity in the club’s league position despite the passage of time and personnel changes.

In addition to the match report, the content includes reader correspondence from the "Football Daily" email service. Bob Dunning shared an anecdote about West Ham players Mervyn Day and Bill Green, noting that both were in the West Ham United team from 1976-78 and featured in Carlisle United’s 1974-75 season. Dunning observed that Green played against Day while at Carlisle, creating a "Green Day" connection, though he noted the band had not yet formed.

Tim Russell contributed a comment regarding musical football matchups, suggesting it was a shame Gareth Barry was at Manchester City a few years too late to play alongside David White. Tommy Boyd offered a separate aside about attending matches at the old Highbury in the late 1960s, where he and others were entertained by a local constabulary brass band at every first team game. The text concludes by identifying this material as an extract from the daily football email, directing readers to a specific page for the full version.
summary: Dejan Kulusevski played his first match for Tottenham in 526 days as the team defeated Coventry. Ben Davies scored a late deflected goal to move Tottenham up to 16th place.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Eagles QB Jalen Hurts Likely to Miss Rest of Season After Blood Clots Detected
content: The Eagles quarterback’s recent health issues highlight how football’s toughness culture puts its players at risk Jalen Hurts is likely to miss the rest of the NFL season after an ultrasound revealed blood clots in his lungs. Thankfully, he’s now restricted from playing for the immediate future, meaning he won’t be risking serious complications – or even his life – as he did when he played in the Philadelphia Eagles’ Week 5 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars in London. The quarterback complained to the Eagles’ medical staff of calf pain on 8 October, according to ESPN. The Eagles say Hurts flew to London with the rest of the team and, out of an “abundance of caution”, was given an ultrasound. The test found a superficial clot in his calf. Doing an ultrasound before the flight would’ve been the most prudent thing. The same for making him inactive after the clot was found. But instead, he played in the game on 11 October, as the medical staff and doctors in London agreed “that activity and mobility were important”. Hurts also practiced all last week before a follow-up ultrasound also found clots in his lungs.
summary: Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts is likely to miss the rest of the NFL season after an ultrasound revealed blood clots in his lungs. He played in the Week 5 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars in London on October 11 despite a calf clot that was discovered during a preflight ultrasound.
author: Guardian Sport

title: PETA urges Crystal Palace to retire live bald eagle mascot
content:
Peta has urged Crystal Palace to retire its American bald eagle mascot, Phoenix, saying the match‑day experience can leave the bird “frightened, disoriented and panicked” and put spectators at risk.  

In a letter to the club’s chief executive, Sharon Lacey, the animal‑rights group called on Palace to end Phoenix’s appearances at Selhurst Park and to commit never again to use a live animal mascot.
summary: PETA urges Crystal Palace to retire live bald eagle mascot.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Golden bat or ball: does cricket need an equivalent to the Ballon d’Or? | Taha Hashim
content:
Football’s annual Ballon d’Or has become a cultural obsession. The award is presented at the London Palladium, and this month the ceremony featured Harry Kane, Lamine Yamal and Lionel Messi. The discussion quickly shifts to next year’s contenders, with a BBC headline in July noting that a World Cup final could be pivotal in the race. The controversy reached a peak when Real Madrid boycotted the 2024 ceremony because Vinícius Júnior had to settle for a silver medal – a move that was described as a “team” decision.

In contrast, cricket celebrates individual achievements across a broader spectrum. The sport highlights milestones such as hundreds, five‑wicket hauls and batting or bowling averages, and it even invites forensic analysis of whether Joe Root will overtake Sachin Tendulkar as the leading run‑scorer in Test history. The International Cricket Council maintains rankings for the best batters, bowlers and all‑rounders in men’s and women’s formats.

On a lighter note, the author’s Instagram feed was recently hijacked by AI bunnies breakdancing, adverts for hair‑loss pills, and a ranking of the best Test batters of the century by Stuart Broad and Jos Buttler.
summary: Golden bat or ball: does cricket need an equivalent to the Ballon d’Or? | Taha Hashim.

title: Tottenham coach De Zerbi says team lacks confidence but is good after win over Coventry
content: Tottenham Hotspur head coach Roberto de Zerbi praised his side’s spirit and attitude after the club secured its first Premier League win of the season, defeating Coventry City. He acknowledged a lack of confidence but stressed that the team remains a good one.
summary: Tottenham Hotspur head coach Roberto de Zerbi praised his side’s spirit and attitude after their first Premier League win of the season. The victory came against Coventry City, and De Zerbi said the team lacks confidence but remains a good team.

content: Mark Allen’s return to competition concluded in defeat at the Northern Ireland Open. The big-name player lost to Jordan Brown during the tournament held at the Waterfront Hall, becoming the latest prominent competitor to exit the event.

content:
Ronnie O'Sullivan faces a battle to remain in the world’s top 16 rankings.  
A World Championship without him would be hard to conceive after years of his central role at the Crucible, yet that scenario may not be far away.

content: United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby supported national wealth and inheritance taxes in a Sunday interview with The New York Times. He argued these measures would help level the playing field for Americans, stating that wealth inequality has become a danger to society and must be addressed by the federal government.
summary: United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby backed national wealth and inheritance taxes in an interview published Sunday. He said wealth inequality has become a danger to society and that the federal government must address it.

content: Jon Stewart criticized President Trump for signing an executive order that waives Russia sanctions to permit increased diesel imports, describing the action as “insane” and “incoherent.” The waiver reverses a sanctions bill Trump signed into law in September, which Congress had passed with bipartisan support.
summary: Jon Stewart criticized President Trump for waiving sanctions on Russia that allow more diesel to enter the market, calling the move “insane” and “incoherent.” Trump signed an executive order last week that waived the sanctions bill he had signed into law in September.

title: China Accuses U.S. Navy of Illegal Entry Near Disputed Shoal, Deploys Forces
content:
China on Tuesday accused the U.S. Military of “illegally” entering waters around a disputed shoal in the South China Sea, saying it had deployed its own forces to watch a Navy ship.  

China claims roughly 90 percent of the South China Sea as its own territory, a claim that has led to disputes with the Philippines, Malaysia, Vietnam and other regional states.

title: Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, 18, will remain in jail after terror attack plot charges
content: A federal judge ruled that 18‑year‑old Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, who was arrested in Minnesota on accusations of planning a terror attack at the Mall of America in Minneapolis, must remain in jail. U.S. Magistrate Judge Dulce Foster said he would not be released because he poses a risk to the community and is a flight risk, according to the Associated Press.

title: President Trump Announces $8B Program to Pay Farmers One-Time Diesel Cost Offset
content: President Trump announced on Monday a one‑time payment program for farmers, aimed at offsetting diesel costs during this harvest season. The initiative is part of an $8 billion effort, though officials say it likely will not produce an immediate impact.
summary: President Trump announced a program that will give farmers one-time payments to help offset diesel costs this harvest season. The $8 billion program is unlikely to have an immediate impact.

title: Former OpenAI worker accused of bugging conference room planned travel to Saudi Arabia: Prosecutors
content: Federal prosecutors say Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35‑year‑old Saudi national who worked as an engineer at OpenAI, was arrested in early October after allegedly hiding a recording device in the company’s offices. At the time of his arrest, prosecutors claim he was planning to leave the United States for Saudi Arabia.
summary: A former OpenAI employee accused of bugging the company’s offices was planning to leave the U. S.

title: Rhys Morgan captures fin whale footage off Pembrokeshire coast
content:
Amateur wildlife photographer Rhys Morgan filmed a remarkable sighting while sailing off the Pembrokeshire coast in Wales. Morgan and his friends spotted the blowholes of a fin whale in the distance, and the footage was shared online as a video of the large marine mammal.

The whale was identified by its distinctive features: a hooked fin near the tail, a dark‑grey upper body, a white belly, and an asymmetrical jaw that is dark on the left side and white on the right.

Viewers of the video have used the clip to raise awareness that fin whales are being hunted in Iceland, urging government ministers to take action.
summary: Amateur wildlife photographer Rhys Morgan recorded a fin whale while sailing off the Pembrokeshire coast in Wales. Viewers of the video are urging government ministers to act against fin whales being hunted in Iceland.

title: Study finds progestogen reduces autoimmune risk of estrogen-only hormone therapy
content:
Progestogen, a component of hormone therapy, is recognized for its protective benefits to the uterus.  

A new study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of The Menopause Society in San Diego (Oct. 20–24, 2026) suggests that adding progestogen to estrogen‑only therapy limits the increased risk of composite autoimmune disease associated with estrogen alone.
summary: Progestogen is recognized for its benefits in protecting the uterus when used in hormone therapy. A new study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of The Menopause Society in San Diego suggests that adding progestogen limits the increased risk of composite autoimmune disease associated with estrogen-only therapy.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Penn State study shows preschool social skills training boosts adult quality of life
content:
A team of Penn State researchers studied preschoolers who received supplemental instruction focused on social, emotional, and language skills.  

Nearly twenty years later, those children reported a higher quality of life than peers who did not receive the same instruction, according to the interdisciplinary study.
summary: Preschool students who received supplemental instruction to build social, emotional and language skills reported a higher quality of life almost two decades later. The study was conducted by an interdisciplinary team of Penn State researchers.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Huntsman researcher launches melanoma prevention program for at‑risk children
content: Children whose parents have been diagnosed with melanoma face a lifetime risk of developing the disease that is twice as high as the general population. A researcher from the Huntsman Cancer Institute at the University of Utah has created a program that successfully teaches melanoma patients and their children protective behaviors. The initiative focuses on habits that can reduce the likelihood of melanoma onset later in life, providing families with actionable strategies to safeguard young skin.
summary: Children of parents who have melanoma have twice the lifetime risk of developing the disease themselves. A researcher from Huntsman Cancer Institute at the University of Utah (the U) has developed a successful program to teach melanoma patients and their children behaviors that will help prevent the onset of melanoma later in life.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Higher physical activity frequency linked to lower perimenopause symptom burden
content: A recent study reports that higher physical activity frequency is associated with a lower symptom burden in perimenopause. Regular exercise also improves sleep, lowers blood pressure, reduces anxiety, builds muscle, strengthens bones, and helps control weight.
summary: A new study suggests that higher physical activity frequency is associated with a lower symptom burden during perimenopause. Regular physical activity also improves sleep, lowers blood pressure, reduces anxiety, builds muscle, strengthens bones, and helps control weight.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Combined Estrogen and Testosterone Therapy Boosts Lumbar Spine Bone Density
content:
A new study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of The Menopause Society in San Diego suggests that combining estrogen and testosterone therapy may improve lumbar spine bone mineral density compared to estrogen alone. The findings were shared during the conference held from October 20–24, 2026.

The research addresses the significant decrease in bone mineral density that occurs during and after menopause due to dropping estrogen levels. While estrogen therapy has historically been prescribed to protect bones, the study indicates that adding testosterone may yield better results.
summary: The study found that adding testosterone to estrogen therapy increases lumbar spine bone mineral density compared to estrogen alone. Results were presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of The Menopause Society in San Diego, Oct. 20–24, 2026.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study finds astronauts' hearts may handle Mars gravity after six‑month ISS missions
content: A new study led by Northwestern Medicine, UT Southwestern, and UT Houston tracked the heart function of 13 astronauts during roughly six‑month missions aboard the International Space Station. The findings suggest that a trip to Mars may be more feasible than previously thought.
summary: A new study led by Northwestern Medicine, UT Southwestern and UT Houston suggests a trip to Mars may be more feasible. The researchers tracked heart function of 13 astronauts during roughly six‑month missions aboard the International Space Station.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Locusts get sensory assist from nanomaterials to detect more chemicals
content: Scientists have long explored using insects as field agents in environments where humans cannot survive or fit. The concept involves deploying creatures like cockroaches into earthquake rubble to map human chemical signatures, or grasshoppers through minefields to locate bombs based on encountered vapors.
summary: Locusts receive a sensory assist from nanomaterials, enabling them to detect more chemicals. Scientists are exploring the use of insects, such as cockroaches and grasshoppers, to map chemical signatures in hazardous environments like earthquake rubble and minefields.

title: Study asks who benefits from hospital and landfill locations
content: A study asks who benefits from the location of hospitals or landfills. It notes that cities develop around essential public facilities, with some—such as hospitals and parks—being more desirable for residents, while proximity to wastewater plants or landfills is less attractive.
summary: Cities are built around critical public facilities, some of which are more desirable for neighbors than others. People prefer living near hospitals and parks, but living near a wastewater plant or landfill is viewed differently.

title: Oscar Dahlsten's team finds quantum pathway to entropy-free energy transfer
content: A research team led by Oscar Dahlsten, an associate professor in the Department of Physics at City University of Hong Kong, set out to prove a theoretical limitation. Instead, they discovered a quantum solution that breaks traditional physical constraints and offers a new strategy for harvesting energy from fluctuating sources.
summary: A research team led by Oscar Dahlsten, associate professor in the Department of Physics at City University of Hong Kong, set out to prove a theoretical limitation. They discovered a quantum solution that breaks traditional physical constraints and introduces a strategy for harvesting energy from fluctuating sources.

title: Study finds shorter interval between death and reported rebirth in unexpected deaths
content: An analysis of more than 1,600 purported reincarnation cases found a notable correlation: the interval between a person’s death and the reported “rebirth” tended to be shorter on average when records showed the prior individual had died unexpectedly.
summary: An analysis of more than 1,600 purported reincarnation cases was conducted. The study found that the interval between death and reported rebirth was on average shorter when records indicated the prior person had died unexpectedly.

title: Human activity threatens biodiversity in remote Patagonian kelp forests
content:
Marine scientists have carried out the first re‑survey of northern Patagonia’s kelp forests in more than 50 years. The study examined one of the world’s most remote marine ecosystems.

The survey revealed dramatic changes in the kelp forests, which the scientists attribute to human activities that threaten the region’s biodiversity.
summary: Marine scientists conducted the first re-survey of northern Patagonia's kelp forests in more than 50 years. They discovered dramatic changes across one of the world's most remote marine ecosystems due to human activities.
author: Phys.org

title: University of Aberdeen study links ancient warming to prolonged wildfire activity
content:
New research from the University of Aberdeen, published in Scientific Reports, indicates that global warming periods can trigger long-lasting increases in wildfire activity. The study provides the first detailed evidence of how wildfires responded to the Danian hyperthermal, a major natural warming event that occurred approximately 65 million years ago. The findings suggest that ecosystems take significantly longer to recover from such events than previously believed.

This work offers important insights into the risks facing today’s world, where climate change is driving more frequent and severe fires. By analyzing the ancient wildfire data, the researchers highlight the potential for prolonged ecological impacts in a warming climate.
summary: The University of Aberdeen study, published in Scientific Reports, shows that periods of global warming can trigger long‑lasting increases in wildfire activity. It provides the first detailed evidence of wildfires responding to the Danian hyperthermal around 65 million years ago, indicating ecosystems take far longer to recover and highlighting risks for today’s climate change.
author: Phys.org

title: Hokkaido University Scientists Find Blood Sugar–Regulating Peptide in Red Alga
content:
Research led by scientists at Hokkaido University has identified a peptide released during the digestion of a specific red alga. This small protein fragment shows potential benefits for blood glucose control and diabetes prevention. The findings were published in the journal Food Bioscience.

Red seaweed, known as nori in Japan and gim in Korea, is a common dietary staple in Asia, frequently used in sushi, rice wraps, and ramen toppings. Despite its widespread consumption, many of its nutritional benefits have remained poorly understood until this recent discovery.
summary: Hokkaido University scientists discovered that digestion of a particular red alga releases a peptide that may help control blood glucose and prevent diabetes. The study was published in the journal Food Bioscience.
author: Phys.org

title: 1,000 mathematicians pledge to shun AI in research
content: A growing backlash against AI companies’ approaches to mathematical problems has led 1,000 human mathematicians to pledge avoiding AI in their research.
summary: A growing backlash against AI companies' approach to mathematical problems has led to a significant number of researchers opting out. One thousand human mathematicians have pledged to avoid using AI in their research.

title: Your aging brain may be trading memory for something more valuable
content: Scientists suggest the aging brain may be shifting its focus from remembering details to understanding the bigger picture, rather than simply losing abilities. This transformation could be an evolutionary adaptation that helps older adults develop wisdom and share decades of knowledge with younger generations.
summary: The aging brain may be undergoing a remarkable transformation rather than simply losing its abilities, shifting its focus from remembering details to understanding the bigger picture. Scientists suggest this change could be an evolutionary adaptation that helps older adults develop wisdom and share decades of knowledge with younger generations.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists find bizarre Jurassic "squid" relative in Wyoming
content:
Scientists have identified the fattest belemnite ever discovered, a bizarre, barrel‑shaped squid relative that lived in Wyoming’s ancient seas 160 million years ago.  

The exceptionally rare fossils reveal a creature unlike anything previously known, potentially a predator of smaller squid‑like animals and a surprising survivor of a supposedly vanished family.
summary: Scientists identified the fattest belemnite ever discovered, a barrel-shaped creature that lived in Wyoming’s ancient seas 160 million years ago. The rare fossils reveal a potentially predatory animal that is a surprising survivor of a supposedly vanished family.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists discover a surprising link between vitamin C and cancer survival
content: A clinical trial suggests that taking vitamin C daily could improve survival in people with precancerous blood disorders and early‑stage blood cancers. Patients receiving the supplement had fewer adverse events and showed a promising survival advantage, raising hopes that a common vitamin could help protect against leukemia‑related complications.
summary: A surprising clinical trial suggests that taking vitamin C daily could improve survival in people with precancerous blood disorders and early-stage blood cancers. Patients receiving the supplement had fewer adverse events and showed a promising survival advantage, raising hopes that a common vitamin could help protect against leukemia-related complications.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists Measure Helium from First Five Minutes of Universe with Unprecedented Precision
content:
Scientists have achieved a major breakthrough in understanding the Universe’s earliest moments by measuring the amount of helium formed in the first five minutes after the Big Bang with unprecedented precision. An international team utilized one of the world’s most powerful telescopes to conduct this analysis.

The study focused on 15 remarkably pristine galaxies that act as cosmic time capsules, preserving clues from nearly 13.8 billion years ago. This research provides new insights into the conditions of the Universe’s first five minutes.
summary: Scientists measured the amount of helium formed in the first five minutes after the Big Bang with unprecedented precision. An international team used one of the world’s most powerful telescopes to study 15 remarkably pristine galaxies that act as cosmic time capsules, preserving clues from nearly 13.8 billion years ago.
author: Science Daily

title: Improved Hurricane Forecast Graphics Help Identify Threats, Not Action
content: A new study indicates that while improved hurricane forecast graphics help people identify threatened areas, they do not increase the likelihood of recognizing danger or taking protective action. Researchers also highlight that a widespread misunderstanding of the hurricane cone persists, creating a dangerous gap between accurate forecasts and public preparedness.
summary: The study shows that improved hurricane forecast graphics help people identify threatened areas but do not increase their likelihood of recognizing danger or taking protective action. It also finds that a widespread misunderstanding of the hurricane cone remains, indicating a dangerous gap between accurate forecasts and public preparedness.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists Discover Statins Trigger Muscle Pain by Causing Calcium Leak
content: Scientists have identified a mechanism behind statin-induced muscle pain, weakness, and severe muscle damage. Using advanced imaging technology, researchers found that these cholesterol-lowering drugs attach to a crucial protein in muscle cells. This attachment forces open a channel that normally controls calcium flow, causing calcium to leak continuously and potentially damaging muscle tissue.
summary: Scientists used advanced imaging technology to discover that statins attach to a crucial protein in muscle cells. The attachment forces a channel to open, causing continuous calcium leakage that can damage muscle tissue.
author: Science Daily

title: Webb Telescope Reveals Hidden Protostars in NGC 7129 Stellar Nursery
content:
NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope released a new image on October 6, 2026 that showcases the stellar nursery NGC 7129, located about 3,300 light‑years from Earth. The image highlights numerous protostars and stars that were previously hidden behind dense dust clouds. 

In the composite, hot, atomic hydrogen gas appears in a golden hue, while cooler, molecular hydrogen gas—shocked by the embedded protostars—is shown in red. The visual representation was processed by Alyssa Pagan of STScI, and the image credit lists NASA, ESA, CSA, and STScI.

The release invites viewers to learn more about this region and offers an interactive experience that allows a closer look at the cauldron of cosmic creation revealed by Webb.
summary: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has revealed many protostars and stars within the glowing gases of NGC 7129. Hot, atomic hydrogen gas is shown here in the golden region, while cooler, molecular hydrogen gas, shocked by embedded protostars, is represented in red.
author: NASA News

title: Maricopa County Again Focus of Trump‑Backed Election Conspiracy Claims
content: Maricopa County, Arizona, is once again the focus of election conspiracy theories. The article notes that in 2020, the county became the epicenter for claims by then-President Trump that the election was stolen. Six years later, the president and his allies are reportedly reviving their “rigged” narrative ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.
summary: In 2020, Maricopa County was the epicenter of Trump’s claims that the election was stolen. Six years later, the president and his allies are dusting off their “rigged” playbook ahead of the midterms.

title: Spotify Launches Podcast Memberships in 34 Regions
content:
Spotify is beginning to roll out its new Memberships subscription feature in 34 regions, a tool first announced in May that allows podcast creators to earn additional revenue. The platform enables fans to pay for exclusive perks, which include access to additional content, early access to episodes, bonus material, and reduced advertising. Podcasters can set their own pricing options and bundle various benefits across multiple subscriptions.

Users can locate the Memberships option directly on a podcast’s Spotify page. According to Spotify, the process allows listeners to subscribe, pay, and access these exclusive benefits in just a few taps.
summary: Spotify has rolled out a new Memberships subscription feature for podcasts in 34 regions, following its May announcement, allowing creators to offer exclusive content and perks behind a paywall. Fans can subscribe on a podcast's Spotify page and access benefits such as additional content, early access, bonus episodes, and reduced ads.

title: Antigravity Halves A1 Drone Price to $799 with Wristwatch Control Kit
content: The Antigravity A1, with the new Follow Me Kit. | Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge Last year's Antigravity A1 is the best beginner drone I've ever tried. I put a friend who'd never flown into its virtual cockpit and didn't worry one bit. The A1's also nice for people who'd prefer to think about flying rather than filming, because you can reframe its 360-degree footage after. But until today, that meant wearing the company's FPV goggles and spending upwards of $1,599 on the complete set. Now, Antigravity is halving the price of entry to $799 in the US with a new "Follow Me" kit that replaces the original headset and motion controller with a wristwatch and ring instead. The idea is that Antigravity can be your robot cam …

title: Square Enix Launches First HD-2D Final Fantasy Game, Resonance
content:
Square Enix announced the launch of its first HD‑2D Final Fantasy title, Resonance, marking a return to the SNES‑era aesthetic.  

The HD‑2D style blends detailed pixel art with 3D graphics, a technique previously used in remakes of early Dragon Quest games.  

While the series has expanded to blockbuster entries such as Final Fantasy XVI and the Final Fantasy VII Remake trilogy, Resonance targets fans of classic retro RPGs.
summary: Square Enix is launching its first HD-2D Final Fantasy game, titled Resonance. The title continues the retro RPG style with pixel art and detailed 3D graphics, appealing to fans of early Final Fantasy titles.
author: The Verge

title: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort Brings Wii Sports Back to Switch 2
content:
Wii Sports remains a landmark in Nintendo’s history.  It is the company’s best‑selling piece of software, a title that permeated culture in unexpected ways and helped rejuvenate Nintendo after a period of steady decline.  

The original game also launched one of Nintendo’s most important and unassuming franchises.  While later sports titles have not matched its sales, they have become a fixture on each new console, comparable to a new Mario Kart or Pokémon release.  

The Switch 2 now offers its own version, Nintendo Switch Sports Resort, which reviewers say is the best sports title available on the platform to date.
summary: Wii Sports, Nintendo's best-selling software, helped rejuvenate the company after a period of steady decline and kicked off one of its most important franchises. The Switch 2 now offers Nintendo Switch Sports Resort, a new version of Wii Sports that is considered the best so far.
author: The Verge

title: Adobe adds one‑tap AI eye‑opening to Lightroom mobile on iOS, iPadOS and Android
content:
Adobe has announced that the mobile version of Lightroom, available on iOS, iPadOS, and Android, now includes a new generative‑AI tool that can open closed eyes in photos with a single tap. When the app detects a person—or a group of people—whose eyes are closed, it automatically displays an “Open Eyes” Quick Action icon over the image, giving users immediate access to the feature.

The ability to restore a subject’s eyes has been part of Adobe’s Photoshop Elements for nearly a decade. According to DPReview, Elements achieves this by sourcing the replacement from another photo, a detail that highlights how the new Lightroom function builds on a long‑standing capability.
summary: Adobe announced that the mobile Lightroom app for iOS, iPadOS and Android can now open closed eyes in photos using generative AI with a single tap. When closed eyes are detected, the app displays an Open Eyes Quick Action icon over the image, offering a feature previously available in Photoshop Elements.
author: The Verge

title: TikTok staff warned of child safety risks, executives ignored concerns
content:
TikTok employees informed executives about significant child safety risks on the platform, according to court records obtained by NPR. Staffers expressed frustration that leadership failed to adequately address their concerns, which included minors bypassing age-restricted content and appearing in "transactional sexual content" from which the company could financially benefit.

These previously unreported depositions were filed in federal court in March as part of a multi-district litigation initiated in 2022. The consolidated legal action brings together hundreds of lawsuits alleging issues involving TikTok, Meta, and Snap.
summary: TikTok staffers warned the company about child safety risks, including minors bypassing age restrictions and appearing in transactional sexual content. Executives failed to act on these concerns, according to court records filed in March as part of a multi‑district litigation that began in 2022.
author: The Verge

title: Spotify removes over 50 million AI‑generated slop and spam tracks from recommendations
content:
Spotify announced that it has removed more than 50 million songs it identified as AI‑generated “slop” or spam from user recommendations over the past year. The company said it has also updated its recommendation system to give greater visibility to music created by human artists.

According to the statement, Spotify’s editors maintain the same standards and do not program content flagged as slop or spam into recommendations. The company reports that, since making these changes, there has been a marked decrease in listener concerns about such content appearing in their suggestions.

While Spotify has not required labels on all AI‑generated tracks, it introduced an “AI Persona” badge to identify music that was created with artificial intelligence.
summary: Spotify announced it deleted more than 50 million AI‑generated slop or spam songs from user recommendations in the past year. It also updated its recommendation system to favor human‑made music, reported fewer listener concerns, and introduced an “AI Persona” badge without requiring labels on all AI tracks.
author: The Verge

title: FedEx Truck Stole Over $963,000 Worth of Graded Pokémon and Sports Cards
content:
Over 200 packages of graded trading cards were stolen last week from a FedEx truck parked outside the Professional Sports Authenticator (PSA) headquarters in Santa Ana, California. According to a report by The Athletic, the packages were being shipped back to their owners when they were taken. PSA, identified as one of the largest third-party sports and hobby card grading companies in the world, reported the incident to the Santa Ana Police Department.

The company stated that the majority of the stolen packages had an approximate value exceeding $963,000. However, PSA noted that this figure could increase as the company continues to confirm exactly which cards were included in the shipment.
summary: Over 200 packages of graded trading cards were stolen from a FedEx truck parked outside the headquarters of Professional Sports Authenticator (PSA) in Santa Ana, California. The majority of the stolen packages were valued at more than $963,000, and the total value could increase as PSA confirms which cards were taken.
author: The Verge

title: Meta Muse AI agent exposes private data through guessable share links
content: Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through Web links, researchers reported Monday. Like many online services, Muse allows users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed. A single query is all that's required Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. After opening a few hundred of them, the researchers found information that was clearly not intended to be publicly available, including: Read full article Comments
summary: Researchers from Claroc reported that Meta's Muse AI agent allows users to share conversations via Web links that are easy to discover. The security firm enumerated 6,800 such links and found sensitive personal and business information that was not intended for public access.
author: Ars Technica

title: Oura Introduces Advanced Workout Metrics to Differentiate Amid Rising Smart Ring Competition
content: Oura has introduced new fitness metrics designed to illustrate how workouts affect the body. This move aims to help the company differentiate itself as the smart ring market becomes increasingly crowded. The innovation comes amid growing competition from rivals such as RingConn and Ultrahuman, which are challenging Oura’s long-standing dominance in the sector.
summary: Oura is launching more advanced workout metrics to show how workouts impact your body. The company aims to differentiate itself from competitors such as RingConn and Ultrahuman as the smart ring market becomes more crowded.
author: TechCrunch

title: Eka Robotics valued at $1.45B thanks to a physical AI model that has experts raving
content: Eka Robotics is valued at $1.45 billion, a valuation attributed to its physical AI model that has experts raving. The company claims its robotic arm may be the first to reliably pick a wide range of objects, performing with smooth, human‑like motion that is impressing the industry.
summary: Eka Robotics is worth $1.45B thanks to a physical AI model that has experts raving. Its robotic arm may be the first to pick a wide range of objects smoothly and human-like, wowing the industry.
author: TechCrunch

title: CTO Madhu Shashanka: AI lacks human judgment despite task proficiency
content:
Madhu Shashanka, co-founder, chief scientist, and chief technology officer at data security software company Concentric AI, argues that while artificial intelligence is becoming proficient at specific tasks, it cannot replace human judgment. Shashanka highlights the current state of AI by pointing to autonomous vehicles, which, despite being among the safest options built, frequently receive easily avoidable parking tickets.

According to the Wall Street Journal, Waymo vehicles crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles. However, these cars remain clumsy at basic tasks, such as avoiding disabled parking spots, tow-away zones, or steering clear of church garages during Sunday services. Shashanka describes this dynamic as AI being impressively capable at complex issues yet embarrassingly clumsy at simple ones. This disparity has significant implications for determining which aspects of work will remain human-driven and which will be automated.
summary: CTO Madhu Shashanka: AI lacks human judgment despite task proficiency.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Labor and Coalition Set to Bet on AI as Community Trust Falls
content:
Australian workers expect the government to act to protect them from AI harms, and a clear reform solution is available. Labor and the Coalition are increasingly moving toward a rare consensus, with both parties wanting to take a major bet on artificial intelligence. However, this political alignment is occurring as community support for the technology collapses.

Last year, only 30% of Australians believed the benefits of AI outweighed the risks. In 2026, community trust in AI appears to be falling even further, creating a disconnect between the parties’ strategic direction and public sentiment.
summary: Labor and the Coalition are moving toward a major bet on artificial intelligence, while Australian workers expect the government to protect them from AI harms. Community trust in AI has fallen, with only 30% of Australians believing its benefits outweigh risks last year and trust falling further by 2026.
author: Guardian Technology

title: 71-Year-Old Illinois Man Throws Rock at Smart TV After Frequent Updates
content: Is your television listening to every conversation? Filling your home with highly invasive ads? Some viewers have had enough of tech violating their privacy When Dan had had enough of his television, he threw a rock straight through the screen. The offence? His smart TV was downloading its third update in three days. “It drove me crazy with what seemed like daily software updates that never fixed anything and ‘features’ that never seemed to work,” says the 71-year-old from Illinois. “And of course, constantly trying to push me to subscribe to paid-for services when all I wanted to do was watch over-the-air TV, play a DVD or stream something from my computer.” Some may accuse Dan of being a luddite, but his master’s degree in computer science and decades of experience in telecommunications would suggest otherwise. “The tech is not intimidating,” he explains, “just increasingly enshittified.”
summary: Dan, a 71-year-old Illinois resident, threw a rock through his smart TV after it downloaded its third update in three days. He complained that the frequent updates added useless features and pushed paid services, despite his background in computer science and telecommunications.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Computer program Darmok outperforms humans on Times cryptic crossword
content:
When the IBM supercomputer Deep Blue defeated Garry Kasparov at chess in 1997, it marked an early triumph of artificial intelligence over human skill and the culmination of decades of research. Almost 30 years later a similar milestone has been reached in a different arena: cryptic crosswords.

Earlier this month a computer model named Darmok solved the final puzzle of the Times’s annual cryptic crossword competition about three minutes faster than Liam Hughes, 29, who had become the contest’s youngest human winner. The program’s speed and accuracy surpassed the best human performance in the event.

The Times competition, known for its challenging clues, has now seen a machine outperform its top human competitor. This development echoes the historic Deep Blue moment and suggests that artificial intelligence is extending its reach into more complex, language‑based puzzles.
summary: A computer program has finally oudone humans at solving cryptic crosswords. Plus, more from around the puzzleverse • Don’t get Cluesletter, our weekly puzzles newsletter, delivered to your inbox?
author: Guardian Technology

title: US government bans Chinese startup DeepSeek AI tools for agencies
content:
The U.S. government has issued a directive ordering all federal agencies to cease using artificial intelligence tools developed by the Chinese startup DeepSeek. The directive, released by the Department of Homeland Security, cites concerns that the use of these tools could result in the transfer of sensitive data to China.  

The notice specifically bans products created by DeepSeek and any third‑party tools built on DeepSeek technology. Agencies are required to remove such products from their information technology devices immediately.
summary: US government bans Chinese startup DeepSeek AI tools for agencies.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Elon Musk’s SpaceX Impact on Ukraine Sparks Debate Over Tech Power
content:
TechScape, a newsletter that examines how technology shapes our lives, was launched by the Guardian. The latest issue is written by Blake Montgomery, the Guardian’s US tech editor, who is composing the piece while viewing Roy Lichtenstein’s monumental Drowning Girl in New York City. The newsletter invites readers to sign up to receive future editions.

In the current edition, Montgomery discusses the dangers of technology having too much influence over society. He highlights SpaceX’s impact on Ukraine, the growing divide between artists and fans over AI‑generated music, and the broader question of how much control technology should exert on everyday life.

Montgomery also examines the risks associated with Elon Musk’s one‑man global infrastructure, and notes that the Guardian is hosting an AI conference in Paris, which will explore similar concerns about the power of tech billionaires.
summary: Today’s TechScape issue discusses the perils of Elon Musk’s SpaceX influence in Ukraine, AI‑generated music, and a Guardian AI conference in Paris. Critics are asking what happens when technology has too much control over our lives.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Google Cloud outage in UK disrupts courts and banks, millions affected
content:
Google’s cloud services experienced a significant outage in the United Kingdom, disrupting a range of online operations. The failure affected the company’s London‑based cloud computing operations, specifically the europe‑west2‑b zone, and was attributed by Google to a “power event” that occurred on Tuesday.

The outage had a broad impact: UK courts were unable to conduct hearings, and customers of major banks—including Lloyds, HSBC, and Revolut—were unable to access or send cash. Millions of users reported that they could not access or move money during the disruption.

Services were restored for most users after the incident, but the power fault had already stalled court proceedings and left many banking customers without access to their funds.
summary: Google Cloud outage in UK disrupts courts and banks, millions affected.
author: Guardian Technology

content: Donald Trump has used the unrest in France as a campaign message ahead of the November 3 U.S. midterm elections. He has seized on the situation to attack immigration policy and criticize the Democrats.

title: Zelensky in Oslo for talks with US envoys as Ukraine says missiles delayed
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Norway Tuesday to meet with US envoys in order to put diplomacy back on a "more constructive path”, Oslo officials said. Relations between Kyiv and Washington have deteriorated since US President Donald Trump reached an agreement with Moscow last week to purchase Russian diesel and Zelensky accused the US of delaying the planned delivery of interceptor missiles.

title: French PM Lecornu blames ultra-left groups for weekend riots, pledges massive security
content:
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu told the National Assembly on Tuesday that authorities will deploy a “massive” security presence next weekend. He said the decision follows announcements by protest organisers of new demonstrations.

Lecornu also accused ultra‑left groups of fomenting an “insurrection” that sparked riots last weekend. He linked the unrest to nationwide protests over the cost of living and education funding.
summary: French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu told the National Assembly on Tuesday that authorities will mobilise a massive security presence next weekend after organisers announced plans for new protests. He accused ultra‑left groups of fomenting an insurrection that led to the past weekend’s riots during nationwide demonstrations over the cost of living and education funding.

title: French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin vows harsh penalties for weekend rioters
content:
Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said the rioting that occurred this weekend in France exposed shortcomings in how security services dealt with threats from looters. He pledged that those involved in the unrest would receive “extremely firm” punishment.

FRANCE 24’s International Affairs Editor Angela Diffley provides additional coverage of the minister’s comments.
summary: The weekend's rioting in France highlighted security services' handling failures, Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said. He promised that rioters would face extremely firm punishment.

title: France examines responsibility for October 17 riots and proposed bill to charge vandals
content: A review of the October 17 riots in France examines who is responsible for the violence that erupted that day. The analysis identifies the participants as “casseurs,” or lawbreakers, and notes a proposed bill that would require them to pay for the damage they caused. It also reports that the French government has issued a mea culpa while political parties engage in a blame game, and a controversy is emerging over whether the vandals were “ultra‑left” members.
summary: The October 17 violence in France involved casseurs, or lawbreakers, whose identity is debated. A bill is being proposed to make the vandals pay for the damage, while the French government has issued a mea culpa amid a political blame game over whether the perpetrators are ultra‑left.
author: France 24

title: French PM Sebastien Lecornu promises massive police deployment for Saturday protests
content: French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu told parliament on Tuesday that authorities will mobilise a “massive” security presence for new demonstrations scheduled for Saturday. He said the deployment follows organisers’ announcement of fresh protests after riots broke out on the sidelines of earlier nationwide demonstrations, and noted that the security operation for the previous protests had been “too static and not mobile enough.” FRANCE 24’s Luke Shrago reported the statement from Place de la République in central Paris.
summary: French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said authorities will mobilise a massive security presence for new demonstrations planned for next Saturday. He said the security operation for last weekend's protests had been too static and not mobile enough, after organisers announced protests following riots on the sidelines of nationwide demonstrations.

content: France in Focus’s latest edition examines the demanding world of French sommellerie. Reporters track Pascaline Lepeltier as she undergoes intensive preparation for the World’s Best Sommelier competition. title: Trump approval rating drops to record low 31% as Republicans face midterm risk
content: US President Donald Trump’s approval rating has fallen to a record low of 31%, prompting heightened concerns among Republicans ahead of the November midterm elections. title: UN World Food Programme ends aid for over 500,000 Palestinians in Gaza after cuts
content:
Sweeping aid cuts have forced the United Nations World Food Programme to end monthly assistance for more than half a million Palestinians in Gaza, the agency’s director for Palestine said. The reduction comes as winter approaches, a period expected to deepen hunger. Two‑thirds of Gaza’s population now face crisis‑level food insecurity, and 200,000 people are reported to be in danger of famine.

More than a year after a Trump‑brokered ceasefire took effect, promised reconstruction has not begun, jobs remain scarce, and the vast majority of residents continue to rely on aid for food.
summary: Two-thirds of Gaza's population face crisis levels of food insecurity and 200,000 people are in danger of famine. Aid cuts forced the UN World Food Programme to end support for more than half a million Palestinians each month.

title: People scour Strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran attacks 15 container ships
content:
At least 15 container ships were struck in the Strait of Hormuz in the past 10 days after Iran’s attacks. Rumors that the vessels carried valuable goods have led people to scour the waterway for spilt cargo.

The attacks included drone strikes and mines. A recent incident on Sunday involved a rocket‑propelled grenade launched from a small boat that struck a ship 75 miles (120 km) northeast of the Saudi port of Jubail.

The incidents highlight the ongoing risk to shipping traffic in the crucial waterway, prompting people to search for any cargo that may have fallen into the sea after the strikes.
summary: Iran attacked at least 15 container ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz in the past 10 days. People have been scouring the waterway for spilt cargo, with ships hit by drones, mines and a rocket‑propelled grenade from a small boat 75 miles north‑east of the Saudi port of Jubail.

title: Houthi missile strike kills 53 at Yemen government training camp, biggest loss since war restart
content:
A ballistic missile launched by Houthi forces struck al‑Alam training camp in the Jardan district of Shabwa province, killing at least 53 people. The attack, described by Yemen’s UN‑recognised government as a disaster, represents the deadliest single loss of life since the civil war resumed in September.

More than 200 individuals, identified as mostly young recruits from the government security forces, were injured in the strike. The wounded were transferred from the police and army training camp to a hospital in Ataq, the provincial capital, where officials appealed for blood donations to treat the casualties.
summary: At least 53 people were killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on the al‑Alam training camp for Yemeni government security forces in Shabwa province. More than 200, mostly young recruits, were injured and taken to a hospital in Ataq, where pleas for blood donations were made.

title: Israeli police detain 10 settlers in rare West Bank raid after photojournalist attack
content: Move comes after US photojournalist and group of European diplomats and Palestinians were assaulted in separate attacks Israeli police have detained 10 people in a rare raid against settlers, after a weekend of extreme violence in the occupied West Bank including an attack on US photojournalist Heidi Levine, which she described as an “attempted lynching”. She was knocked down, kicked and beaten by a group of masked Israeli men as she covered the olive harvest in a Palestinian village on Friday. The militants broke four vertebrae and a rib, ripped open her finger so it required surgery and left her with lacerations across her body.
summary: Israeli police detained 10 people in a rare raid against West Bank settlers following a weekend of extreme violence in the occupied territory. The violence included an assault on US photojournalist Heidi Levine, who was knocked down, kicked, beaten and suffered broken vertebrae, a broken rib, a finger injury requiring surgery and multiple lacerations.

content:

The operation, described as the most significant military mission signed off by Andy Burnham as prime minister, will involve RAF pilots attempting to shoot down Houthi missiles and drones that have targeted Saudi airports and oil facilities.

title: Ryanair chief Michael O’Leary predicts European fares could rise up to 20% in 2027
content:
Ryanair chief executive Michael O’Leary warned that European air fares could increase by as much as 20% in 2027. He linked the projected rise to higher jet‑fuel costs driven by the conflict in the Middle East, noting that many airlines have not hedged against such price spikes.

O’Leary also said the fuel‑price pressures could trigger airline bankruptcies and takeovers as carriers struggle with the higher operating costs.

title: Unconditional £2‑a‑day income to Peruvian Amazon Indigenous people aids rainforest protection
content: A study of a pioneering unconditional basic‑income pilot in the Peruvian Amazon found that providing Indigenous participants with a daily payment of £2 helped protect the rainforest. Researchers reported that almost 90 % of those receiving the income adopted practices that were environmentally beneficial. The analysis, conducted by the University of Bath, is intended to inform the ongoing debate about the effectiveness of direct payments to communities that steward globally important ecosystems.
summary: A pilot unconditional basic income scheme gave Indigenous people in the Peruvian Amazon £2 a day. Researchers reported that almost 90% of participants adopted environmentally beneficial practices, helping protect the rainforest, in a University of Bath analysis.

title: Michael Kiwanuka releases new album 'Fudge' recorded in Southampton studio
content: (Polydor) Its release delayed by ill health, Kiwanuka’s latest was made in tandem with 2024’s Small Changes – but it’s much more than a mere companion album In November 2024, Michael Kiwanuka released his fourth album, Small Changes, an extremely poised and self-assured piece of work. After three gold albums, a Grammy nomination, a Mercury prize win and the ongoing success of Cold Little Heart, a 2017 single hoisted to virality and million-selling status in the US after its use in TV drama Big Little Lies, Kiwanuka – and his long-term production collaborators Danger Mouse and Inflo – evidently felt confident enough to release a beautiful but wilfully understated album. Recorded in LA, some impressive names lurked in the credits: legendary session musicians including bassist Pino Palladino and the drummer James Gadson, who played on Marvin Gaye’s I Want You and Donald Fagen’s The Nightfly; the similarly legendary R&B producer Jimmy Jam served as organist on three tracks. It attracted the kind of critical praise in which adjectives like “unhurried” and “meditative” figured heavily. But it also wasn’t the whole story. It turned out there was a second album, its songs written – or rather, jammed into existence by Kiwanuka and members of his live band – concurrently with Small Changes. It was made not in LA but in a studio that “looks like a medieval hut” in Southampton. August session musicians and legendary R&B producers were not present during its recording, nor were Danger Mouse and Inflo. Indeed, you could read its opening track, Summer Clothes, as a kind of Dear John letter to both of them (“I’m OK, I found another way … we’ll be back here soon, just not today”).
summary: Michael Kiwanuka's new album 'Fudge', recorded in a Southampton studio, was made concurrently with his 2024 album Small Changes and was delayed by ill health. The album's opening track, Summer Clothes, serves as a "Dear John" letter to collaborators Danger Mouse and Inflo.

title: Charles Burnett Discusses Chronicling Black Working-Class Life and Dilemma at 1983 Film Release
content: A restored version of his 1983 film My Brother’s Wedding, set in South Central LA, brings Burnett’s vision to a new audience Charles Burnett had a dilemma. He had agreed to attend the wedding of a co-worker, but the wedding was scheduled for the same day and time as a funeral for a childhood friend. Initially, the film-maker – a landmark chronicler of Black working-class lives – decided he’d go to the funeral. But when he tried to break the news to the co-worker, she was so dejected that he couldn’t go through with it. He tried asking the bride to change the wedding – which was “ridiculous to think of trying to do”, he says decades later – but that didn’t work either. He decided he’d go to both events.
summary: A restored version of Burnett's 1983 film My Brother’s Wedding, set in South Central LA, is bringing his vision to a new audience. Burnett faced a dilemma between attending a co-worker's wedding and a funeral for a childhood friend, ultimately deciding to attend both events.

title: Selma Blair denies intent to harm during Delta flight incident
content:
Actor Selma Blair was arrested after a Delta Air Lines flight from Los Angeles to New York, where she allegedly assaulted two cabin crew members, a police officer and a nurse. The incident reportedly involved a medical emergency on the aircraft, during which Blair allegedly injured the crew.

In a statement released on Friday, Blair’s representatives said the episode was a medical emergency and that she did not intend to hurt anyone. They dismissed earlier media coverage as unsympathetic and inaccurate, specifically criticizing reports that she tried to open the airplane door while passengers were aboard.
summary: Actor Selma Blair was arrested after a Delta Air Lines flight from Los Angeles to New York on allegations that she assaulted cabin crew, a police officer, and a nurse. Her representatives say the incident was a medical emergency and that she did not intend to hurt anyone.

title: Ali G discusses backlash over return in interview held at Staines chicken shop
content: Staines’s finest nailed the zeitgeist of the late 90s and early 00s, and now he’s back – but how does he fit into 2026? He discusses the backlash against his return, his worst ever interviewee and how he’s going to prevent world war two “Can you tell people that you’re from Hustler?” Ali G asks me. “Or The Source. Or Guns & Ammo. Speaking to a Guardian journalist ain’t a good look for me in the hood.” At Ali’s request, we are meeting in an independent chicken shop in Staines because – due to some sort of mix-up – he thought the one interview he had agreed to for his new film was Chicken Shop Date, which was “90% likely to lead to boning”. He follows this with an entirely unprintable reminiscence about the first time he and “me Julie” had sex in the disabled toilets of Egham KFC.
summary: Ali G talks about the backlash to his return and his plan to prevent world war two. The interview, which he mistakenly thought was for his new film Chicken Shop Date, took place in an independent chicken shop in Staines.

title: Elizabeth Holmes documentary 'You Can See Everything' opens to $15m on 855 screens
content:
Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary, You Can See Everything, achieved a record-breaking $15 million domestic box office debut across 855 screens. According to production company A24, the nearly three-hour film about Elizabeth Holmes generated over 2,000 sold-out screenings during its opening weekend. This performance marks the largest opening weekend for a documentary in North America since Fahrenheit 9/11 in 2004.

The film’s earnings also set a new benchmark for limited releases, becoming the biggest opening for a movie playing on fewer than 1,000 screens since Borat earned $26.5 million in 2006. The $15 million total translates to approximately A$21.5 million or £11.2 million, underscoring the significant audience demand for the buzzy title despite its limited theatrical footprint.
summary: Elizabeth Holmes documentary 'You Can See Everything' opens to $15m on 855 screens.

title: The Simpsons gives Apu Nahasapeemapetilon a new voice with Sunil Malhotra
content:
The Simpsons has returned the long‑silent character Apu Nahasapeemapetilon to the airwaves, giving him a new voice after eight years without dialogue. American actor Sunil Malhotra, who moved to the United States from India as a child, stepped into the role and made his first appearance on the animated series on Sunday night.  

Malhotra described the moment as “his homecoming,” noting that he is replacing Hank Azaria as the voice of the beloved character. The change marks a significant shift for the show’s longstanding cast.
summary: After eight years of silence, The Simpsons has given longtime character Apu Nahasapeemapetilon a new voice. American actor Sunil Malhotra, who moved to the US from India as a child, made his first appearance as Apu on Sunday night.

title: Podcast series explores two men sharing a heart, same wife and gunshot deaths
content: How did two men who shared the same heart and the same wife end up dying the same way? Plus, inside the beef between ‘the Kennedys of Italy’ This fascinating series opens with the death of a man from a gunshot wound – and the revelation that this isn’t the first time his heart has stopped beating. It previously belonged to another man who died the same way, and who also had the same wife. Hosted by Karen Kilgariff, what follows is an intriguing eight-part tale that veers between a scientific exploration and a gripping true-crime saga. Alexi Duggins Apple, from Monday 19 October
summary: Podcast series explores two men sharing a heart, same wife and gunshot deaths.

title: Why Galaxy Quest is a feel‑good film that dismantles cynicism
content:
In the latest installment of a series that highlights the most easily rewatched comfort films, the writer offers an appreciation of Galaxy Quest. The film is described as a smart, funny, and tender ode to fan culture, celebrating its affectionate and humorous take on fandom.

The piece centers on the line, “By Grabthar’s hammer, by the sons of Worvan … you shall be avenged.” For viewers of the movie, the quote can be moving. It marks the moment when Alan Rickman’s character—a Shakespearean lover turned sci‑fi sidekick—realises that the ludicrous catchphrase he has reluctantly uttered thousands of times does matter after all.
summary: The article praises Galaxy Quest as a smart, funny and tender ode to fan culture. It notes the scene where Alan Rickman’s Shakespearean‑style sidekick realizes his repeated catchphrase “By Grabthar’s hammer, by the sons of Worvan … you shall be avenged” finally matters.

title: Brock Purdy becomes highest-rated passer in NFL history as 49ers stay perfect
content:
The San Francisco 49ers defeated the Washington Commanders 23-17 on Monday night, improving their record to 6-0 for the sixth straight win of the season. Quarterback Brock Purdy threw a touchdown pass, while Christian McCaffrey ran for two scores to lead the offense. The Niners built a 20-point lead and secured the victory with two late defensive stops against the Commanders, who finished with a 1-4-1 record.

This victory allowed the 49ers to follow up an emotional win at division rival Seattle the previous week. The game marked a significant milestone for Purdy, who became the highest-rated passer in NFL history as his team remained unbeaten.
summary: The San Francisco 49ers beat the Washington Commanders 23-17 to stay 6-0 for the season. Brock Purdy threw a touchdown pass and Christian McCaffrey had two rushing scores in the win.

title: Ten Hag Accuses Ronaldo of Letting Team Down at Manchester United
content: Ten Hag says Ronaldo did not complete post-match run Former manager claims club broke promises made to him Erik ten Hag has claimed Cristiano Ronaldo “let the team down” during their time together at Manchester United. Ten Hag has also alleged that promises made by United’s owners went unfulfilled, leading to his sacking by United in October 2024. Ronaldo returned for a second spell at United in August 2021 and was already at the club when Ten Hag was appointed as Ole Gunnar Solskjær’s successor in 2022. content: Ghana may soon come calling for Trinidad and Tobago’s former captain and manager, who is proud of his CV since his days as a Premier League striker Dwight Yorke wants you to stop calling him a former player. “I’m not a kid trying to get into management for the first time,” he says from his home in Dubai. “I’ve done that and I want that message to come across clearly.” The message has a deadline. Carlos Queiroz left his job as Ghana head coach on 1 October and the Ghana Football Association is searching for his successor. Yorke is among the names under consideration, along with Pape Thiaw, Aliou Cissé and Walid Regragui, the former Morocco head coach, according to Ghanaian media.

title: Canada defeats England's Red Roses in first loss in four years
content: A first defeat in four years could be liberating for England after so long fighting to preserve their historic unbeaten run England’s glittering unbeaten era is over. Canada defeated the Red Roses to deal them a first defeat in four years after 40 wins and one draw. It was a landmark result for the Canadians, who will look to replicate the outcome this weekend when the two nations meet again. England must reset but they won’t panic; the Red Roses have been the standard bearers for the past seven years, which is why they have lost only twice in 73 matches. But while no team would ever aim to lose, falling to defeat is a good thing for England and the wider sport. Losing could actually make England a deadlier team to face. That is because they now need to find another level to their game with teams beginning to figure out ways to beat them. They have been pushed over the past few years by teams such as Canada, New Zealand and France, but they always had just enough to get the result over the line. Now they have been presented with a new challenge and John Mitchell, who lost his first game as Red Roses head coach, said post-defeat when his side “gets a setback, it generally learns quicker”.
summary: Canada defeated England's Red Roses, giving the team its first loss in four years after a streak of 40 wins and one draw. Red Roses head coach John Mitchell said the setback would help the team learn faster.

title: Steven Guilbeault urges Cop17 to prioritize nature action despite global crises
content:
Steven Guilbeault reflects on his childhood in La Tuque, Quebec, where he protested the felling of trees behind his home by climbing one while his mother deflected developers’ requests. This memory resurfaced in December 2022 during the final hours of a global agreement in Montreal. Nearly 200 countries reached a consensus to halt and reverse the loss of nature by 2030, a milestone Guilbeault helped facilitate. He emphasizes that nature is a critical asset for health, food security, and economies, rather than a peripheral concern.

Despite global wars and economic pressures that may frame environmental protection as optional, Guilbeault argues that nature cannot wait for more favorable conditions. He urges that Cop17 must deliver tangible action, noting the widespread passion and inspirational power of nature conservation worldwide. The article serves as a call to prioritize immediate environmental measures over distractions posed by other international crises.
summary: Steven Guilbeault states that nature is a critical asset that cannot wait for a better year, even when wars and economic pressures distract from it. He references his role in pushing through the 2022 international agreement to protect biodiversity and emphasizes that Cop17 must deliver real action.

summary: Australia’s updated cardiovascular disease risk calculator is identifying substantially more Australians aged 45–74 as being at intermediate risk of heart attack and stroke.
